newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's Soekor to sell oil tanker by tanker.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's Soekor to sell oil tanker by tanker.

text.p: South Africa's Soekor (Pty) Ltd plans to sell oil from its Oribi field on a tanker by tanker basis initially, company officials said on Thursday.

They said no contracts had been signed yet for the oil, production of which is due to start at the end of March after delays in preparing the semi-submersible production rig in Simonstown shipyard. The original target date had been February.
"Basically the idea from our side is we will sell it to get the best price, and we think that can be done on a tanker by tanker basis," John Hawkes, chief Soekor engineer on the rig, told Reuters.

"Obviously there have been discussions with the refineries in Cape Town and Durban, but it will be on a tanker by tanker basis unless they tie up a long-term contract after the first shipment or two, but that's still open."
The two producing wells at Oribi will pump 20,000 barrels per day which will loaded onto a million-barrel capacity tanker for shipment to Cape Town or Durban.
"So you're looking at a tanker-load about every six weeks," Hawkes said.

"Our oil (quality) actually exceeds Brent crude, it's got good viscosity and almost no sulphur at all. We anticipate it would certainly fetch the price of Brent and it should actually trade at a premium to Brent," he said.
Hawkes said the shipyard work on the rig had taken longer than anticipated due to problems with weather, labour, the Christmas holidays and "teething trouble".
Soekor is spending $75 million on the rig from purchase to production and hopes to recoup the investment within the first year.
The Oribi field has an estimated lifespan of three to six years, but Hawkes said satellite fields were being tested and some could be brought into production in two years.

He said the rig was due to be towed out of harbour on Monday for sea trials and should be in place over the wells off Mossel Bay by the end of January. Work at the site would take two months before production started.
The oil will be South Africa's first commercial-scale output and is will be equivalent to about six percent of South African consumption.
